title: Final exam: DP, BFS on numbers, knapsack, anagrams
overview: The course's final exam problems. Two ask for the same sequence in top-down and bottom-up style. One turns 'can I reach N?' into a BFS over numbers. One is a straight 0-1 knapsack with several test cases, and the last is an anagram check by sorting.

concepts.explain: The same recurrence can be memoized recursion or a forward loop. Bottom-up avoids deep recursion and is natural when every smaller value is needed anyway.
Each term is the sum of the previous **four**, starting with 0, 1, 1, 2. Four base cases are needed.
In 'reach N from 1 by +3 or x2', each number is a node and each operation is an edge. BFS with a `vis` array explores every reachable number up to N once.
Both operations only increase the value, so anything bigger than N can never come back down. Don't push it.
With many test cases, clear `dp`/`vis` before each one, for the full range the test uses.
Two words use the same letters exactly when their sorted forms are equal.
concepts.snippet: sort(a.begin(), a.end()); sort(b.begin(), b.end()); return a == b;

files.title: Tetranacci Number I (top-down)
files.what: Memoized recursion for the Tetranacci sequence, as the problem requires recursion.
steps: `memset(dp, -1, ...)` marks every value as unknown.
Base cases: n <= 1 returns n, n == 2 returns 1, n == 3 returns 2.
If `dp[n]` is known, return it.
Otherwise store the sum of the four previous terms.

files.title: Tetranacci Number II (bottom-up, long long)
files.what: The loop version for n up to 60, using `long long` because the values pass the `int` limit.
steps: Create `long long tetra[n+1]`.
Set the first four terms: 0, 1, 1, 2.
For `i = 4..n`, add the four previous terms.
Print `tetra[n]`.
files.output_note: Prints `208`, the same as the top-down version.
files.watch_out: For n < 3 the array has fewer than 4 cells, yet the code writes `tetra[3]` (and `tetra[2]`, `tetra[1]`), which is out of bounds. It may still print the right value by luck. Size the array `max(n + 1, 4)` or declare it with a fixed size like 65.

check.q: Why is `long long` needed here but not in version I?
check.a: Version I stops at n = 30, which fits in int. Terms near n = 60 are far larger than 2^31.

files.title: Make it (BFS over numbers)
files.what: Starting from 1 you may add 3 or double. BFS from 1 over all values up to N tells whether N can be reached.
steps: Push 1 into the queue and mark `vis[1]`.
Pop a value `par`; if it equals `n`, return true.
Try `par + 3` and `par * 2`; push each one that is at most `n` and unvisited.
If the queue empties, return false.
Clear `vis` before each test case.
files.complexity: Time O(N) per test · Space O(N)
files.input_note: T, then T values of N. This is the judge's sample.
files.output_note: `YES NO YES NO YES`, one per line (for example 5 = 1 x 2 + 3, and 16 = 1 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2).
files.watch_out: Clearing all 100005 cells of `vis` per test is wasteful with 1000 tests; clearing only `vis[0..n]` is enough. Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`; this file relies on another header bringing it in.

check.a: From 1 you can get 4 or 2; every later value is at least 4 or is 2 (which leads to 5 or 4). Nothing lands on 3.

files.title: Adventure (0-1 knapsack, many tests)
files.what: Memoized 0-1 knapsack, repeated for each test case, with the dp table reset correctly (capacity 0..W inclusive).
steps: Read `n`, `max_weight`, then all weights, then all values.
Reset `dp[i][j] = -1` for `j` from 0 **through** `max_weight`.
`knapsack(i, w)`: 0 if no items or no capacity; memo check; take/skip choice.
Print `knapsack(n-1, max_weight)`.
files.complexity: Time O(N·W) per test · Space O(N·W)
files.input_note: T; each test: N W, the weights, the values. This is the judge's sample.
files.output_note: Prints `13` and `28`, matching the sample. In test 1, items of weight 3 and 4 give 7 + 6 = 13.
files.watch_out: Weights can be 0 here, and the base case is `max_weight == 0`. With capacity 0 a weight-0 item with value > 0 would be missed; `if (i < 0) return 0;` alone is the safer base case.

check.q: What changed from the buggy Module 15 versions that makes this one correct?
check.a: The reset loop uses `j <= max_weight`, so the starting state is really marked as unsolved.

files.title: Pile of Word (anagram check)
files.what: Sort both words and compare them letter by letter; equal sorted words are anagrams.
steps: Sort `s1` and `s2` (they are copies, so the originals are unchanged).
Different lengths: return false.
Compare each position; any difference means false.
Otherwise return true and print YES.
files.complexity: Time O(L log L) per test · Space O(L)
files.input:
4
eat tea
madam madam
ball all
ant tan
files.input_note: T, then T lines with two words. This is the judge's sample.
files.output_note: Prints `YES YES NO YES`, matching the sample. `ball` and `all` differ in length.

check.q: How could you check anagrams in O(L) instead?
check.a: Count each letter in an array of 26: add for the first word, subtract for the second, and check that all counts are 0.

recap: One recurrence, two styles: memoized recursion or a bottom-up loop.
Match the integer type to the constraints (n = 60 needs `long long`).
'Can I reach N with these operations?' is a BFS over numbers.
Reset DP/visited arrays for every test case, over the full range.
Sorted strings are equal exactly when the words are anagrams.

check_yourself.q: In Make it, why is it safe to ignore values above N?
check_yourself.a: Both operations only make the number bigger, so a value above N can never come back to N.

check_yourself.q: How many base cases does a recurrence that uses the previous k terms need?
Is 10 reachable in Make it? Show a path.
